claims.claim: The roadmap forbids ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children and requires manual one-at-a-time teardown, while the deletion PRD commits to `strategy.deletionOrder` with `AllAtOnce` and `Reverse`; PRD author `@ranakan19` must resolve which ApplicationSet deletion contract governs the workstream before implementation proceeds.

The standing incident rule requires `AllAtOnce` before any child Application is deleted manually, but the deletion PRD plans a `Reverse` mode that performs sequential child deletion; `@ranakan19`, as the deletion PRD owner, must hold the `Reverse` rollout until the controller fix replaces that interim restriction.

The maturity plan freezes `strategy.rollingSync.steps` as one `matchExpressions` match-set per step at Stable, while the parallel-steps workstream proposes multiple concurrent match groups inside a step; the Progressive Sync Stable owner, currently only identified as the pair owning the Stable punch list, must either land parallelism under a new field before Stable or exclude it from the frozen v1 API.

The impersonation rollout decision requires a per-project flag and prohibits enabling it until the diff path is fixed, while the impersonation RFC specifies only the system-level `applicationcontroller.enable.impersonation` switch applying to every Application; RFC owner `@anandf` must revise the enablement design before the rollout can proceed under the adopted restriction.

Hydrator pilot repositories are prohibited from using Progressive Sync until a debounce exists, but the T-27949 pilot workstream explicitly runs Source Hydrator commits through `RollingSync`; because neither the restriction nor the ticket names an owner, the hydrator and Progressive Sync program leads must assign one before that pilot can continue.

The rollout decision changes impersonation from the RFC's system-level switch to a per-project flag. After enablement, the destinationServiceAccounts-selected service account performs sync and diff, Kubernetes audit events must record both the requesting and impersonated identities, and the Argo CD admin who controls the AppProject mapping must review that access; leaving governance tied to the old fleet-wide applicationcontroller.enable.impersonation setting would miss project-specific grants.

Server-Side Diff does not consistently follow the destinationServiceAccounts identity used by sync: the external-cluster path acts as the cluster Secret credential, while the reported CI path acts as argocd-server or the destination service account depending on impersonation behavior. This splits one application's actions across identities and pressures reviewers to grant standing cluster credentials real patch authority that Kubernetes cannot restrict to dry-run; auditors therefore cannot assess least privilege from the AppProject mapping alone and must correlate Kubernetes audit events for the cluster credential, requesting Argo CD identity, and impersonated service account.

The namespace-boundary request requires the Argo CD control-plane identity to perform CreateNamespace and the impersonated service account to perform repository-driven sync without permission to apply kind: Namespace, but the impersonation design applies the per-Application destination service account to all sync resources and all kubectl commands. The current model therefore cannot satisfy that access-control request: the AppProject admin reviews only one destinationServiceAccounts grant, and the Kubernetes audit trail cannot evidence the requested resource-class separation because no separate acting identity is selected for Namespace resources.

Hydrated commits are pushed by the GitHub App credential, while commitAuthor merely copies the dry commit's human attribution; with commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits disabled by default, neither the branch nor hydrator.metadata proves which identity produced the hydrated content. Enabling the proposed cluster-wide signing key would make signatures attributable to any principal able to read Secrets in the Argo CD namespace, so access review must cover both the repository-write GitHub App credential and signing-key readers, not the human named in commitAuthor.

provenance-and-authorship: Hydrated commits are machine-generated and pushed with a GitHub App credential, while `commitAuthor` merely copies the dry commit's claimed human author; because signing is opt-in and currently defaults off, neither the hydrated branch nor `hydrator.metadata` proves whether the human or the app authored the rendered content.

The roadmap's published commitment that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented cannot coexist with the PRD's proposed `strategy.deletionOrder` supporting `AllAtOnce` and `Reverse`; shipping the PRD would reverse the stated teardown commitment.

licensed-review: Licensed counsel in the jurisdiction governing the project's contributor and user terms should determine whether the roadmap's manual-deletion statement or the PRD's ordered-deletion proposal constitutes a binding published commitment, and whether the unsigned GitHub App commits and copied `commitAuthor` metadata satisfy applicable authorship and audit-record requirements; this issue-spotting draft does not replace that review.

The ApplicationSet roadmap commits teardown to manual, one-Application-at-a-time operation and explicitly excludes ordered or automated deletion, while the Progressive Sync deletion PRD commits to `strategy.deletionOrder` with `AllAtOnce` and `Reverse`; the ApplicationSet roadmap owner must decide whether ordered deletion is in scope.

The impersonation RFC commits the feature flag to system-level enablement for all Applications, while the rollout decision requires a per-project flag; the impersonation feature owner must choose the supported rollout boundary before release.

The impersonation RFC requires GitOps Engine to honor impersonation for all kubectl commands, but field evidence shows Server-Side Diff does not consistently use `destinationServiceAccounts`: the CLI path can use a narrower service account unexpectedly while the external-cluster reconciliation path uses the cluster Secret credential instead. The impersonation product owner must define and enforce one identity rule for diff.

Reverse deletion commits to deriving one unambiguous order from a strictly sequential `rollingSync.steps` list, but the parallel-steps proposal would allow concurrent match groups and the Stable-promotion ticket will freeze the current steps shape; the Progressive Sync Stable owner must either reject parallel groups or introduce a new ordering field before Stable.

Unobservable in production at fleet scale: a generated `Application.spec` change can leave RollingSync `status.applicationStatus` Healthy without creating a sync operation, but there is no counter for `specChanged` without a resulting sync. The requested progressive-sync metrics cover detection-to-trigger latency, step duration, ApplicationSet-caused refreshes, and wait reasons, so Stable promotion lacks the baseline needed to measure this failure rate before and after the fix.

Unobservable in production except through manual status inspection: reverse deletion can restart a RollingSync wave when a child remains Progressing, flipping the Application between Deleting and Syncing, but no controller-level alert or transition counter records the loop. A before/after evaluation of the controller fix therefore needs a new count of deletion-wave restarts or repeated Deleting-to-Syncing transitions per ApplicationSet.

Observable in production per Application but not measured fleet-wide: when Server-Side Diff ignores `destinationServiceAccounts`, the existing signals are Kubernetes audit identities, `ComparisonError` logs, and repeated Synced-to-Unknown status changes. No metric records diff authorization failures by effective identity or resource kind, so operators cannot quantify how often the diff path bypasses the impersonated service account or establish a baseline before changing it.

T-26271's missing-permissions failure is the CI diff symptom of the impersonation design selecting one destination service account per Application: server-side diff dry-runs cluster-scoped resources under that narrower identity instead of the cluster Secret credential.

T-28695 exposes the other diff-path symptom of the same destinationServiceAccounts design: sync uses the selected impersonation identity, while external-cluster Server-Side Diff falls back to the cluster Secret credential and consequently requires patch permission for every compared resource kind.

T-28511's delete/re-create wave loop is tied to Reverse deletion's explicit wait for each Application to be fully deleted: a child held in Progressing prevents that wait from completing while the ApplicationSet controller recreates the manually deleted child.

T-26443's stale-manifest auto-sync is a symptom of push-to-stage separating hydrateTo from syncSource: hydration writes a fresh commit to the staging branch, but Argo CD continues watching the deployment branch and can sync its previous contents before the external promoter moves the new commit.

T-24417's inability to use a Helm repository chart as DrySource follows from the hydrator design restricting drySource to one Git repository with repoURL, targetRevision, and path, and directing external charts toward Helm dependencies instead.

T-28755's request for parallel groups is the filed symptom of Reverse deletion's ordering invariant: rollingSync.steps is designed as one strictly sequential list of match groups, so independent cluster groups cannot advance concurrently without removing the single order that Reverse depends on.

proposals.change: Record the confirmed root cause: with impersonation enabled, diff runs as the destination service account, whose lack of patch permission on cluster-scoped resources causes the missing-permissions failure; the cluster Secret credential is not the cause.
proposals.citedLine: the CI diff failures (the missing-permissions one, T-26271) got root-caused on the call: with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch on cluster-scoped stuff. someone should note the root cause on that ticket so the reporter stops chasing the cluster secret.

proposals.change: Record that History & Rollback work is deprioritized until next quarter and its development pair has been reassigned to the progressive-sync deletion loop.
proposals.citedLine: hydrator rollback work (the history & rollback ticket, T-27327) is deprioritized to next quarter. dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead. ticket should say so.

proposals.change: Record that the delete/recreate loop was reproduced in staging with reverse deletion order and document the interim runbook mitigation: switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before manually deleting a child Application.
proposals.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

proposals.change: Record that every hydrator push restarts the rolling-sync wave and that hydrator pilot repositories must not use progressive sync until debounce support exists.
proposals.citedLine: the wave-restart thing on hydrated repos: we confirmed each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce. the pilot ticket (T-27949) should carry that restriction so the next team doesn't trip it.

deltas.body: Impersonation must roll out behind a per-project flag rather than fleet-wide, and it must not be enabled for any project until the diff behavior is fixed.
deltas.citedLine: impersonation rollout: we decided it goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed. that's a real decision, not a maybe.
